tour.title: Did God Pour Wrath on Jesus? Teachers on What the Cross Accomplished
tour.intro: You're asking one of the live wires of Christian theology, and the teachers in this corpus do not all answer it the same way — which is exactly why it deserves a tour rather than a single clip. I've ordered these so you first get a map of the atonement theories, then the Old Testament word behind "wrath" and "propitiation," then two opposing ways of reading the same verses, then what Jesus' own cry from the cross is doing, and finally a teacher who tries to hold the pieces together. You'll hear where they agree and where they genuinely disagree — and you can decide what you think.

steps.why: The map before the territory. Two teachers walk through why atonement theories exist at all — they answer "how does the death of one innocent man, albeit you know God's son, how does the death of one man cover or take away the guilt of the entire world?" — and they lay out the major models, starting with the early church's Christus Victor ("Christ is the victor"), then moving toward satisfaction and penal substitution. Listen to this first so every later clip has a place on the map.

Before anyone can argue about whether wrath was poured out on Jesus, you need the word behind the fight. Heiser shows that hilasterion appears in only two New Testament places (Romans 3:25 and Hebrews 9:5), recounts the scholarly standoff — C. H. Dodd arguing for expiation (removal of guilt) against Leon Morris arguing for propitiation (appeasing God's anger) — and then goes back to the Old Testament root to argue it means "purge, it means to decontaminate," concluding that "the point of its use... would be that Christ's blood provides access to God's presence." This is one whole side of the disagreement, argued from the lexicons up.

The direct "yes" to your question, from the same verse Heiser just unpacked. This teacher reads Romans 3:25 against the Day of Atonement: the cross is "the ultimate mercy seat," and "the wrath of God that sin deserves, in some sense, is satiated, in some sense satisfied when Jesus died for our sins." Here God's just repayment for sin "was caught up in and poured out on Jesus Himself." Put this next to the Heiser clip and you have the disagreement in its sharpest form — same text, opposite frame.

Now the direct "no," spoken plainly: "you won't find a sentence in the Bible that says God punished Jesus. Or that Jesus suffered the wrath of God... I've both I have held that view for a long time until I had read the Bible a lot, and then I intentionally went on the search and I couldn't find that." He explains why the wrath-on-Jesus scheme is so popular — it "solves a problem for people" — then reads Romans 8:1-4 to conclude that "what God is punishing is not Jesus, he's punishing evil in the Jesus." A teacher who once believed the view you're asking about, explaining why he changed.
steps.episodeTitle: Day of the Lord Question & Response

steps.why: If the New Testament doesn't say God poured wrath on Jesus, what does "the cup" mean? This clip answers from the story itself: Jesus Barabbas the freedom fighter goes free while Jesus of Nazareth "puts himself in the place of rebellious Israel" before Rome — "the guilty Jesus is let free... while the innocent Jesus, Son of the Father, dies." On the cup of God's anger: "there's never a moment in the Gospels or anywhere in the New Testament that says Jesus suffered the wrath of God," and Jerusalem still fell, so the cup was never a transaction that stopped history. A political-historical reading that stands deliberately against the Protestant tradition it names.

The most visceral evidence people cite for the wrath view is the cry, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — so you need to hear what teachers do with that line. These two read it as Jesus reciting Psalm 22 from the cross: "when he's saying this one line on the cross, he's saying... I'm including everything else that this psalm says by kicking it off with this one line." The cry is a lament of trust — "My God" even inside the forsakenness — not a record of divine abandonment. A different lens on the same words, and a necessary counterweight to step three.

Wright has been accused of denying penal substitution, so he states his position directly: "there is a New Testament doctrine of penal substitution," and Romans 8:1-4 is "clearly penal and clearly substitutionary" — but it "doesn't belong within the narrative that Western Christianity has characteristically told, which is about an angry God wanting to punish somebody and fastening upon his own innocent son." He warns that caricature makes God "just a monster," especially for abuse survivors, then says the larger picture in which substitution sits is "a picture of victory, the victory won on the cross." A middle position that refuses the either/or.

The tour's landing: how one teacher holds the models together. Wright argues it isn't "either Christus Victor or some form of substitution" — "victory through substitution," with the Gospels doing it by narrative rather than theory ("Jesus takes the place of Barabbas"). And on the line in the hymn, "the wrath of God is satisfied": "it's actually decontextualized and it can easily sound as though this is just a malevolent, angry God," so "every other time you sing it, please sing the love of God was satisfied." After hearing both sides argue, this is the synthesis to measure them against.
steps.episodeTitle: #34 An Evening With NT Wright live in London

tour.closing: So: did God pour out wrath on Jesus? You've now heard teachers answer yes (the cross as the mercy seat where sin's due wrath was satisfied), teachers answer no (no New Testament sentence says God punished Jesus; the cup is Jesus taking Israel's place before Rome), and a teacher who says the truth in the penal-substitution tradition is real but has been badly framed. Notice what they share: every one of them insists the cross accomplished something real, that God was in it, and that it was love at the center — the disagreement is over whether the operating picture is a courtroom, a battlefield, an exile-road, or all three. Let the tension stand while you listen; the texts they argue over are worth knowing either way.

caveats: Clips on ad-inserted hosts (Megaphone: ask-nt-wright, spoken-gospel) can land up to ~2 minutes off against today’s stream. This is a known corpus-wide drift, not a bug in this tour.
A tour is model output over machine transcripts. The "why" text should report what a transcript says; it is not a claim that the speaker is right.

The player streams each episode straight from its publisher. A few hosts (Substack’s CDN, for one) refuse hotlinked requests and the step will say so and offer the URL instead — the clip boundaries are still good, the playback path is not.
